name: Dutch Reformed Church
transcript:
Stand where you can see both the clock and one side of the Dutch Reformed Church. If you came in from one of the surrounding streets, think back to the moment you first saw the tower. That view was built into the plan of Aberdeen. The church occupies an eight-sided piece of ground. Four streets lead towards it. Long before anyone put a clock up there, the people laying out the village had given this corner of the Karoo a centre.

The congregation began in eighteen fifty-five. For farming families in this district, attending church in Graaff-Reinet meant a journey. When they established a congregation on the farm Brakkefontein, they adapted the farmhouse for worship. Picture the difference in scale. A room in a house could give neighbours somewhere to pray together. A purpose-built church could bring families from across the district under one roof. The foundation stone for that church was laid in eighteen fifty-nine.

Here is something you could walk around the building and easily miss. Part of the earlier church is still inside the shape you see today. Imagine looking down on the roof from above. The main body and its two side arms make a cross. Architects call the arms the transept. When the church was enlarged, the earlier building became part of that crosspiece. Someone standing there today can be in the later church and in the footprint of its predecessor at the same time.

Now look up from the arms to the clock tower. It belonged to the expansion of nineteen oh seven, roughly half a century after worship began in the farmhouse. At about fifty metres, the tower has a different audience from the entrance below. A doorway addresses the person about to step inside. A clock face that high addresses a whole street. Turn your back to it for a moment and look along the approach. Think how far down that street someone could stand and still read the hour.

Before you leave, pick out one of the much smaller towers on the arms of the church. Follow its outline and then let your eye climb the main tower again. Those repeated upright shapes help knit the old and new parts together. Down at pavement level, the shape of the grounds does something similar for the town. Walk a little way round the corner and the building presents another face to another street. You have only moved a few paces, but you can see why a photograph taken from one direction tells only part of the story. At the next stop, the town clock gives way to a very different silhouette. Look out for the little beasts on the courthouse roof.

name: Magistrate’s Court & Old Post Office
transcript:
From the pavement on Grey Street, give yourself a small challenge. See if you can find a dragon before you find the front door. The creatures are up on the tiled roof of the old post office and magistrate’s court. They are made of terracotta, a clay shaped and fired until it hardens. Against a bright sky you may see the outline before you see the colour. Once you have found one, come back down to the street and look at the building again. How did a place for collecting letters and hearing cases acquire a roof like this?

The Cape Department of Public Works built this complex in eighteen ninety-eight. Aberdeen already had a magistrate’s court by eighteen eighty. The date of this building marks a new home for public services that people in the district already needed. The complex brought court business, postal business and government offices together. Picture two people arriving on the same morning. One has come for a letter from family far away. The other has been summoned to a hearing. They approach the same public building with very different things on their minds.

Start at the base of the tower. Follow the edges upwards as far as you can. Its eight-sided shape gives it a succession of narrow faces. A flat wall facing you might be evenly lit, while the next face of the tower is already in shade. Higher up, the tower narrows. Above it is a spire, then a rounded, bulb-like detail and a flagpole. From a distance those changes merge into one outline. From here you can take them apart, one by one.

Now follow the edge of the red roof away from the tower. Near the eaves, the roof flares out. Underneath, the masonry looks weighty and firmly planted. Above it, the dragons have narrow shapes with daylight around them. That change in scale is part of the pleasure of this building. The stonework can be appreciated by someone standing at the door. A decoration meant to be seen from across Grey Street needs an outline clear enough to survive the distance.

Heritage writers use several style names for the complex, among them Flemish Revival. You need no catalogue of European styles to enjoy what the builders achieved here. Stand a little to one side and see which part disappears first. The face of the tower changes, a stretch of roof comes into view, and a dragon may vanish against the tiles. That short walk gives a better sense of the building than a straight-on photograph. Please keep to the public pavement and leave entrances clear for people with business here. Our next stop takes that eye for detail to a much smaller stone church.

name: Wesleyan Methodist Church
transcript:
At the Wesleyan Methodist Church, begin with the side wall. The easiest detail to overlook here is the piece of wall that sticks out. It has a name, a buttress. Seen straight on, it might look like a stripe of stone. Seen from a little to one side, you can make out its depth. Follow the line of the wall past the windows and look for the next one. On a building with a simple rectangular plan, these projections give the long side a rhythm you can almost count as you walk.

This church dates from the early eighteen eighties. The regional heritage guide places the laying of its foundation stone in eighteen eighty-two and its consecration the following year. Those occasions marked different things. A foundation stone recorded a commitment to build. Consecration marked the setting apart of a finished place for worship. Between those moments came work that seldom makes it onto a commemorative stone. Someone had to set out the walls, bring the materials, prepare the openings and give a roof its support.

Look at one of the arched windows. Begin where its straight sides start to curve, then follow the edge upwards. Making an opening in a stone wall poses a practical question. What holds the masonry above the gap? In a masonry arch, shaped pieces bear against one another and carry the load towards the sides. A buttress adds depth where a wall needs support. Those are useful ideas to keep in mind even when you cannot see the inner construction. They give a reason to look closely at the relationship between the solid stretches of wall and the openings for light.

Now turn to the bell tower. At its top the material changes. The belfry has delicate cast-iron openwork. Look for the sky showing through it. Against the stone below, that small patch of open sky makes the top seem remarkably light. To make cast iron, molten metal is poured into a mould. Curves and repeated shapes can be made together. The eye reads them as something like lace, even though the material is metal. If the light is behind the church, this may be the best detail of all to see in silhouette.

Imagine standing in a neighbouring street when a bell sounded here. People who could see little of the church could still share in the timetable of its congregation. Now bring your attention back to the modest length of that side wall. The rectangular outline, the regular windows and that unexpected crown of iron give the Wesleyan church a character of its own. Carry the shape of one of its windows in your mind. At All Saints, you will have another chance to look at how a congregation used an arch to make a place for worship.

name: All Saints Anglican Church
transcript:
At All Saints Anglican Church, choose one window you can see comfortably from the public approach. Trace it with your eye, starting at the bottom of one side. Go up the straight edge, around the curve and on to the point. Now follow the other side back down. That meeting of two curves is one of the easiest ways to recognise the Gothic Revival character of this little church. Once you have seen it in a single opening, step back until you can take in the length of wall around it.

The regional heritage guide dates All Saints to eighteen eighty-four. Think of where that places it in the walk. The Dutch Reformed congregation had been established for nearly thirty years. The Methodist community had recently built its stone church. By the middle of the eighteen eighties, an Anglican congregation too had made a lasting place for itself in the streets of Aberdeen. A visitor who only saw the great clock tower might never guess how many different places of worship belonged to this small town.

Gothic Revival can sound like a grand term for a quiet building. Here is a way to make sense of it. Nineteenth-century builders returned to forms familiar from much older churches, especially pointed arches. The point gives even a narrow opening an emphatic upward direction. Look at the stone on either side of the window and then at the empty space framed by it. One gives the wall its weight. The other invites your eye through the wall and into the building. From outside, the glass may look dark. A person sitting inside on the same morning receives the daylight coming the other way.

Consider what that means during a service. Someone arriving through the door turns towards the place from which the prayers or readings are led. Windows along a side wall can bring light to the congregation without everyone having to face directly into the sun. Even from the street you can ask which openings would receive morning light, and which might stay in shade. The answers will depend on where you stand and when you visit. Give the building a few seconds of your own attention before walking on.

There is another detail worth carrying away, and it belongs to the name. All Saints is a dedication with room for people whose names may never appear on a plaque. Baptisms, marriages, funerals and ordinary Sundays can give one building a place in many family histories. If the church is closed, you can appreciate much of its design from outside. Take one last look at the pointed window you chose at the beginning. At our next stop, a private house uses light and coloured glass for an altogether different purpose.

name: Pagel House
transcript:
At number seventeen Stockenstrom Street, look for the veranda before you look for the name of the house. The veranda wraps around the building. Follow it with your eye to the point where it turns the corner. That turn makes a difference to anyone living here. A person sitting outside can move from one side to another as the sun travels across the sky. An ordinary route from door to garden becomes a sheltered place to spend part of the day.

The house dates from eighteen ninety-seven. Its first name was Claremont House, and its early owner, R. C. Logie Junior, traded in ostrich feathers. Locally, houses of this kind are sometimes called ostrich villas. A fashionable feather worn far from the Karoo might have passed through the hands of someone who lived on this street. When you look at the breadth of that veranda and the care given to its details, you are seeing one way the feather trade left a mark on the town.

One feature described by the guest house is a sheltered sitting nook with stained glass. Think how different that is from a plain sheet of clear glass. Clear glass leaves the garden as the principal thing to look at. Coloured glass makes the opening itself part of the decoration. As the angle of the sun changes, so does the light reaching the seat. Indoors, the property description records painted pressed ceilings and yellowwood flooring in several rooms. A pressed ceiling gets its pattern from a design impressed into sheet material. Details like these can be appreciated without going inside a private guest room.

How, then, did Claremont House become Pagel House? The name came through a later owner, Frank Wilke. He kept a private zoo near Aberdeen and admired the circus performer Wilhelm Pagel. Pagel was known both as a strongman and as a trainer of large animals. His travelling circus was familiar to South African audiences for decades. After his death, Wilke arranged with his widow to acquire marble plaques bearing the Pagel name. It is this connection that explains the name visitors encounter here today.

Think of the house as keeping two quite different records. Its plan and fittings tell you about a family home built in a prosperous trading town. The plaques tell you about a later owner, his admiration for a performer and the journeys an object can make after its first owner dies. From the pavement, look back once more at the corner of the veranda. On a second visit you might remember the circus first. The shaded seat is a reminder that people also came here simply to sit down at the end of the day.

name: Aberdeen’s Historic Homes
transcript:
For this stop, find two neighbouring homes that you can see from the public pavement. Choose a modest one as well as a house that catches your eye straight away. Begin at the front gate of each, and imagine the short walk from the street to the door. Is the door close enough for someone on the stoep to greet a passer-by? Is there a garden between the street and the veranda? Before you have named a single architectural style, you have already noticed something important about how these houses work.

Aberdeen offers an unusual opportunity to make that comparison. A survey by the Vernacular Architecture Society of South Africa recorded more than two hundred houses in the town dating from before eighteen ninety. That is a remarkable number of ordinary dwellings to set beside the grand villas most often photographed. A small frontage deserves a careful look. The spacing between a door and two windows may give a house much of its character. Try covering the roofline with the edge of your hand for a moment. What still distinguishes one front from the other?

Now uncover the roof and look along its edge. A gable is the end of a wall that rises up against the roof. A veranda has a different job. It carries shelter out beyond the front wall and makes a usable strip of shade. Some Aberdeen houses have intricate trim along the veranda. You may hear the Afrikaans expression broekie lace used for this kind of ornament. Instead of trying to identify the material from a distance, look at its shadow. A plain board makes a dark band. Pierced decoration lets through small shapes of light, and the pattern can be easier to see on the wall than under the roof.

For examples to put on a walking map, the architectural survey lists De Denne in Darling Street, dated eighteen ninety-four, and Villeria in Grey Street, dated eighteen ninety-nine. Carmen Villa in Porter Street dates from eighteen ninety-eight. The dates are close, yet a date alone cannot tell you how a family used a house. Look for a veranda that turns a corner or a window carefully positioned towards a garden. Those choices can say as much about daily life as a date worked into plaster.

Finish where the resident meets the street, at the boundary. A low wall, a gate or a length of decorative wirework can be the best piece of craftsmanship visible from the pavement. Choose one detail you could sketch from memory. Leave the gate as you found it and keep photographs directed away from open windows. These homes have survived long enough for strangers to admire them because generations of people have continued to live in them.

name: Aberdeen Cemetery
transcript:
At Aberdeen Cemetery, begin with a distinction that matters when you walk among the stones. A grave marks a burial. A memorial may name someone whose body lies elsewhere. The two can look very much alike, particularly when lettering has weathered. Start by reading the words on one stone from the path. Does it say that someone lies here, or does it invite you to remember them? That small difference changes what you can safely say about the person it names.

There is a particular reason to ask the question here. The municipal history records the burial of Commandant Carel van Heerden, who died while trying to obtain horses for the Boer forces. It also records a memorial to twenty-five British soldiers who died in the district. One record takes us to a named individual and a particular errand. The other gathers a number of deaths into a public act of remembrance. Hearing the two together tells us something about the war in Aberdeen without requiring us to assume that every soldier commemorated here is buried under that monument.

The South African War lasted from eighteen ninety-nine until nineteen oh two. Aberdeen lay in the Cape Colony. Some local residents joined the Boer forces even though the colonial authorities regarded them as British subjects. For families here, the divisions could run through familiar streets and between people who knew one another. The reference to horses brings the scale of that conflict down to something quite tangible. A mounted group needed fresh horses to move. What might sound like a small errand in a larger war was a task on which a man could lose his life.

There is also a Jewish burial ground beside the Christian cemetery. Its presence gives another starting point for thinking about the town. Along the route you have seen Christian congregations represented by their churches. A burial ground can preserve evidence of another community even when a visitor has seen little trace of its daily life on the main street. If you can read an inscription from the path, take the time to read the whole line. A family relationship or a place of birth can reveal a connection that a surname alone would never suggest.

Before moving on, let your attention settle on an ordinary family stone. Its maker had limited space. Someone had to decide which names, relationships or few words should be cut into it. Weather can make parts of that choice difficult to read. Leave faint lettering as you find it and give anyone visiting a grave room to be alone. The next stop follows one name associated with this burial ground back to a farm, a water supply and the beginnings of the town laid out around us.

name: Jan Vorster & Brakkefontein
transcript:
Our final stop begins with a name you may encounter at the cemetery, Jan Vorster. Local heritage accounts identify this as his resting place. They also identify him as the owner who sold the farm Brakkefontein to the Dutch Reformed Church. It is easy to shorten that story to a sentence about a town being founded. To see what it meant on the ground, consider three things you have already passed on the route. A place to gather. A street to reach it. And water that could reach a household.

The history of this landscape reaches far beyond a farm boundary. Stone Age material has been recorded in the wider district. Pastoral communities knew where animals could graze and where water could be found. Late seventeenth-century accounts describe a Cape expedition trading for livestock with the Inqua under their leader Heykon. That encounter belongs to a landscape people already knew and used. European stock farming expanded into the region later. By the time a sale of land appeared in church records, generations of people had moved through the Camdeboo for reasons of their own.

In eighteen fifty-five a new Dutch Reformed congregation was established. The farmhouse on Brakkefontein was adapted for worship. In eighteen fifty-seven, plots were auctioned. Imagine the different questions facing the congregation and a prospective householder. The congregation needed a place accessible to families coming in from farms. A household choosing a plot would want to know how to reach the market, where animals could stand, and whether there would be water for a garden.

In eighteen fifty-eight Henry Marriott drew up a town plan. Picture a sheet of squared paper. Most of the streets follow a grid, but in the centre is an eight-sided plot reserved for the church. Four principal streets approach its shorter sides. The plan also provided a market square and an outspan square. To outspan meant to unhitch the animals from a wagon. A market needed space for trade. Travellers needed somewhere for the team that had brought their goods into town. Those two needs took up real space on a map.

Water followed another set of lines. The architectural survey records that about two thirds of the plots were served by water furrows. The Afrikaans word leiwater describes water led along a channel. Think of the difference between seeing water somewhere in a valley and having a channel that can carry it to the edge of your plot. That practical distinction shaped what a family could do with its land.

The settlement took the name Aberdeen from the Scottish birthplace of the Reverend Andrew Murray Senior. When you next see the church tower, look down the street beneath it. The tower came later. The direction of the street, the space around the church and the old routes for water take you closer to the decisions that first gave the town its shape. Thank you for walking through Aberdeen with us.
